body: Sloan, 'Do Stock Prices Fully Reflect Information in Accruals and Cash Flows About Future Earnings?' (The Accounting Review 71(3), 1996; ~4,070 Semantic Scholar citations): the accrual part of earnings is less persistent than the cash part, but investors price earnings as if both were equally persistent. A long lowest-accrual / short highest-accrual decile hedge earned about 10.4% a year in abnormal returns (US 1962-1991), with much of it around later earnings announcements. Green, Hand and Soliman, 'Going, Going, Gone? The Apparent Demise of the Accruals Anomaly' (Management Science 57(5), 2011; ~230 citations) show the hedge return collapsed to roughly zero after about 2001-2003, coinciding with heavy hedge-fund trading on it. Replicated: strongly so in-sample and internationally (Pincus et al. 2007 found it in common-law countries), but the US decay is a textbook McLean-Pontiff case. Use for us: the forensic logic is still valid as a QUALITY and blow-up filter even if the US trading premium is gone. Indian filings are much less mined by quant funds, but untested here, so the premium may survive. Flag companies where profit after tax persistently exceeds CFO, receivable days are rising, and contract assets are swelling. That pairs with our existing Beneish (TATA term) and capitalisation checks. A simple backtest on Indian accruals (CMIE/screener data) is a worthwhile own-research project.
title: Sloan accruals anomaly (TAR 1996): ~10%/yr in 1962-91, then largely disappeared in the US after ~2001
